subject: Art and Culture
sub_topic: Rajput painting schools — Mewar, Kangra, Bundi

concepts.name: Origins and Classification of Rajput Painting Tradition
key_dimensions: Distinction between Rajput painting and Mughal painting — shared ancestry vs. divergence
Two broad sub-classifications: Rajasthani schools (Mewar, Bundi, Marwar, Kishangarh) vs. Pahari schools (Kangra, Basohli, Guler)
Role of Hindu court patronage vs. Mughal court patronage in shaping stylistic divergence
UPSC trap: Kangra is a Pahari school, NOT a Rajasthani school — frequently confused with Mewar/Bundi

concepts.name: Mewar School — Historical Development and Patronage
key_dimensions: Earliest surviving examples: Chawand style under Rana Pratap and successor Amar Singh I (late 16th–early 17th century)
Role of Maharana Jagat Singh I (1628–52) as the most significant patron — commissioned the Rasikapriya and Ramayana series
Influence of pre-Mughal indigenous manuscript traditions (western Indian/Apabhramsha style) on Mewar's early phase
Transition from bold, archaic style to more refined compositions in the 17th–18th century under continued patronage

concepts.name: Mewar School — Stylistic Characteristics and Iconography
key_dimensions: Bold, flat colors — dominance of red, yellow, and green backgrounds; strong outlines
Figures depicted with large eyes, broad faces, and profile perspective — indigenous rather than Mughal naturalism
Thematic focus: Ramayana, Mahabharata, Bhagavata Purana, Gita Govinda, and ragamala paintings
UPSC trap: Mewar style is considered the most 'purely Hindu' and least Mughal-influenced among major Rajasthani schools

concepts.name: Bundi School — Historical Development and Distinctiveness
key_dimensions: Bundi (Hadoti region, Rajasthan) — school flourished under rulers of the Hada Chauhan clan from late 16th century
Influenced by Mughal painting more than Mewar, yet retained strong indigenous identity — considered a 'bridge' school
Closely related to Kota school (Kota was carved out of Bundi in 1625) — UPSC trap: Bundi and Kota are often treated as a combined school
Key patrons: Rao Ratan Singh and later rulers who encouraged both secular and religious themes

concepts.name: Bundi School — Stylistic Features and Thematic Content
key_dimensions: Rich, lush landscape depictions — dark green foliage, flowering trees, lotus ponds; nature as an active compositional element
Distinctive treatment of the sky: layered bands of color (blue, green, gold) — unique among Rajput schools
Thematic specialization: ragamala series, baramasa (twelve months), Krishna Leela, and hunting scenes
Animal depictions — especially elephants and horses — rendered with great vitality; Kota branch later became famous for hunting scenes

concepts.name: Kangra School — Historical Development and Pahari Context
key_dimensions: Emerged in the Kangra valley (present-day Himachal Pradesh) in the mid-18th century; reached its zenith under Maharaja Sansar Chand (1775–1823)
Evolved from the earlier Guler school — transition from Basohli's bold style to Kangra's lyrical refinement
Decline linked directly to Gurkha invasions (1806) and Sansar Chand's defeat — dispersal of artists to other Pahari courts
UPSC trap: Kangra school is NOT the earliest Pahari school — Basohli predates it by nearly a century

concepts.name: Kangra School — Stylistic Characteristics and Aesthetic Philosophy
key_dimensions: Lyrical, delicate, and romantic aesthetic — soft lines, subdued pastel colors, emotional expressiveness (sringar rasa dominant)
Female figures: slim, graceful, with lotus-shaped eyes, arched eyebrows — considered the most refined feminine depiction in Indian painting
Landscape integration: hills, rivers, moonlit nights, and seasonal vegetation are emotionally synchronized with the subject
Strong influence of Vaishnavism — Gita Govinda, Bihari Satsai, Nayika Bheda as primary literary sources

concepts.name: Ragamala Paintings — Cross-School Significance
key_dimensions: Ragamala = 'garland of ragas' — visual personification of musical modes (ragas/raginis) as human or divine figures in specific settings
All three schools (Mewar, Bundi, Kangra) produced Ragamala series — allowing stylistic comparison across schools
Mewar Ragamala (early 17th century): bold colors, flat treatment; Bundi Ragamala: lush natural settings; Kangra Ragamala: lyrical and romantic
UPSC trap: Ragamala is a pan-Indian tradition — also found in Mughal, Deccan, and other Rajput schools — not exclusive to any one school

concepts.name: Gita Govinda as a Unifying Textual Source Across Schools
key_dimensions: Jayadeva's 12th-century Sanskrit poem depicting Radha-Krishna love — the most illustrated text across Rajput and Pahari schools
Mewar illustrations: bold and devotional; Bundi: nature-enriched settings; Kangra: most celebrated interpretation — emotional and lyrical
Kangra's Gita Govinda series under Sansar Chand is considered the pinnacle of Pahari painting achievement
UPSC trap: Gita Govinda was also illustrated in Odisha (palm-leaf manuscripts) — not exclusively a North Indian painting theme

concepts.name: Baramasa Tradition in Rajput Painting
key_dimensions: Baramasa = twelve months — poems and paintings depicting how seasons affect nature and the emotions of separated lovers (viraha)
Bundi school is most celebrated for Baramasa illustrations — rich seasonal landscapes
Literary sources: poems by Keshavdas (Kavipriya, Rasikapriya) frequently illustrated in Bundi and Mewar schools
Connects painting tradition to classical Indian poetic convention of ritu (seasons) as emotional metaphor

concepts.name: Nayika Bheda (Classification of Heroines) in Rajput and Pahari Painting
key_dimensions: Sanskrit aesthetic treatises (Bharata's Natyashastra, Bhanu Datta's Rasamanjari) classify heroines (nayikas) by mood and situation
Kangra school excels in Nayika Bheda depictions — each type rendered with distinct emotional nuance and setting
Bundi and Mewar also illustrated Nayika Bheda — comparison reveals differing approaches to female emotion and sringar rasa
UPSC angle: Nayika Bheda paintings are a bridge between literary theory (rasa) and visual art — demonstrating interdisciplinary nature of Indian aesthetics

concepts.name: Mughal Influence on Rajput Schools — Degree and Nature of Absorption
key_dimensions: Mewar: least influenced — retained indigenous bold style; Bundi: moderate influence (naturalistic elements, court scenes); Kangra: indirect Mughal influence via Guler
Specific Mughal elements absorbed: portrait conventions, landscape detailing, paper medium, and certain compositional formats
Political context: Rajput rulers who maintained greater autonomy from Mughals (e.g., Mewar) also maintained greater stylistic independence
UPSC trap: Mughal influence on Rajput painting is NOT uniform — it varied by geography, patronage, and political relations with the Mughal court

concepts.name: Basohli School — Precursor to Kangra and Its Distinctive Identity
key_dimensions: Basohli (Jammu region) — earliest and most vigorous Pahari school, flourishing in the late 17th century
Distinctive features: intense primary colors (bold red, yellow), beetle-wing cases used to depict jewelry (emeralds), angular facial features
Major work: Rasamanjari series illustrated under Raja Kripal Pal — considered a masterpiece of Basohli style
UPSC trap: Basohli precedes Kangra — Kangra's refinement is partly a reaction to Basohli's boldness, mediated through the Guler school

concepts.name: Role of Krishna Bhakti Movement in Shaping Rajput Painting Themes
key_dimensions: Bhakti movement's emphasis on personal devotion to Krishna directly drove demand for illustrated manuscripts of Bhagavata Purana, Gita Govinda, Rasapanichadhyayi
Mewar's strong Vaishnava identity (Nathdwara as a major pilgrimage center) reinforced devotional themes in painting
Kangra's romantic Krishna-Radha imagery reflects the influence of Bengal Vaishnavism transmitted through Chaitanya's tradition
UPSC angle: Rajput painting is not merely aesthetic but a form of devotional (bhakti) expression — connects Art & Culture to Medieval History

concepts.name: Hunting and Court Scenes — Secular Themes in Rajput Painting
key_dimensions: Bundi-Kota school: most celebrated for dynamic hunting scenes — tigers, lions, elephants depicted with vigorous movement
Court scenes, durbars, and festivals also depicted — providing historical documentation of Rajput courtly life
Mewar school: elephant fights and processions; Kangra: relatively fewer hunting scenes — more focused on romantic and devotional themes
UPSC trap: secular/hunting themes show Mughal influence on compositional dynamism, even in schools that otherwise resisted Mughal aesthetics

concepts.name: Materials, Pigments, and Techniques in Rajput Painting
key_dimensions: Medium: paper (post-Mughal influence) replaced palm leaf and cloth; colors derived from minerals, vegetables, and precious stones
Lapis lazuli for blue, vermillion for red, gold leaf for highlights — costlier pigments indicate royal patronage
Basohli's unique use of actual beetle-wing cases (emerald green) for jewelry — a purely Pahari innovation
UPSC trap: Rajput paintings are predominantly on paper — NOT murals (though mural traditions exist at Bundi's Garh Palace and Mewar's City Palace)

concepts.name: Nathdwara School — Specialized Offshoot of Mewar Tradition
key_dimensions: Nathdwara (Rajasthan) developed as a distinct sub-school focused exclusively on Srinathji (Krishna) devotional imagery
Pichwai paintings — large cloth paintings depicting Srinathji in various seasonal and festive forms — are its hallmark
Emerged after the Vallabhacharya sect established its headquarters at Nathdwara in the 17th century following Mughal religious pressure
UPSC trap: Pichwai/Nathdwara is often listed separately from Mewar school — but it is stylistically and historically an extension of Mewar tradition

concepts.name: Comparative Aesthetic — Mewar (Bold-Devotional) vs. Bundi (Naturalistic-Lyrical) vs. Kangra (Romantic-Refined)
key_dimensions: Mewar: strong lines, flat bold color, frontal figures — devotional energy over naturalism
Bundi: richest natural settings among Rajasthani schools — flora, fauna, and landscape as expressive tools
Kangra: the most 'painterly' of the three — soft gradations, emotional subtlety, influence of classical Sanskrit poetic sensibility
UPSC high-yield: UPSC frequently asks identification questions — knowing the 'signature' visual feature of each school is critical for MCQs and short answers

concepts.name: Decline of Rajput Painting Schools — Causes and Legacy
key_dimensions: Decline in the 19th century due to: loss of royal patronage, British political annexation/subordination of princely states, introduction of photography and lithography
Kangra's decline accelerated by the 1905 Kangra earthquake and the earlier Gurkha devastation under Sansar Chand's defeat
Colonial-era documentation: scholars like Ananda Coomaraswamy (Rajput Paintings, 1916) were instrumental in rediscovering and valorizing these traditions
UPSC angle: Coomaraswamy's role in framing Rajput painting as distinct from Mughal painting is a key historiographical point — connects to nationalism and cultural identity

concepts.name: Ananda Coomaraswamy and the Art Historical Framing of Rajput Painting
key_dimensions: Coomaraswamy's 1916 work 'Rajput Painting' was the first major scholarly treatment — argued Rajput painting expressed a distinctly Hindu spiritual aesthetic
He distinguished Rajput painting from Mughal painting on grounds of spirituality vs. courtly naturalism — a distinction later nuanced by other scholars
His work contributed to nationalist cultural discourse — framing Indian art as having an independent, non-derivative tradition
UPSC trap: Coomaraswamy is associated with Rajput painting's scholarly revival — not to be confused with Percy Brown (Indian Architecture) or Havell (Bengal School advocacy)
